name: Rosa Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a small firm on Market Street in a farming town, and I do farm and land law: selling fields, farm tenancies, and succession plans, which decide who gets the farm when the parents retire or die. I grew up on a dairy farm up the valley; my brother runs it now. Half my week is reading deeds and drafting agreements, the other half is driving out to kitchens with muddy boots by the door. I use the AI tool now and then for letters, once someone else has checked it's safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know these families, and they trust me because they knew my dad. What wears me out is the driving and the pay. I earn less than town lawyers, there's barely another firm doing farm law for thirty miles, and my boyfriend and I can't seem to save a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the farmers I work for were right not to get excited. A tool that saves you ten minutes on a letter is nice, but it doesn't know whose field the stream runs through. I'd say it at the market or at Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's fine for the job, but my money's still tight. I'm paid less than town lawyers, there's barely any other firm doing farm law round here, and we save nothing because nothing's left. That was true before AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing land sales, farm tenancies and succession plans as now. I'd use the AI tool for letters a bit more once the others have shown it's safe. And I'd do my brother's farm accounts in return for meat and eggs, which saves on food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the job, a bit pinched about money. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a succession case that stuck with you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I had three meetings with two brothers who wouldn't sit at the same table. Their father wanted the farm split fairly, and fair meant something different to each of them. I ended up going between two kitchens with a cup of tea in each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing's left. Where does the money go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent on a cottage outside town, diesel for the car because there's no bus, and my student loan. My boyfriend's a mechanic at the tractor dealer, so he's on a modest wage too. We're careful, but careful only gets you so far.

say: I'd say farmers were right **not to get excited**.
I'd say a tool can't know whose field the **stream** runs through.
think: The job is fine, but **money is tight**.
Low pay, **no local rivals** to move to and nothing left to save were there before AI.
do: Keep doing **land sales**, tenancies and succession plans.
Use the **AI tool** for letters more, once it's shown safe.
Do my brother's **farm accounts** for meat and eggs.
S0.quote: A tool that saves you ten minutes on a letter is nice, but it doesn't know whose field the stream runs through.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money**, with costs like **diesel** and rent built into rural life.
Her **farm family** quietly props up the household budget.
She's proud of **local knowledge** that no software holds.

steps.text: Keep handling land sales, farm tenancies and succession plans
Use the AI letter tool once colleagues show it's safe
Do her brother's farm accounts in exchange for meat and eggs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and we should handle it sensibly, without panic and without handouts. Farmers have dealt with new machines for a hundred years. Lawyers can too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the firm takes on fewer young lawyers. The land registry checks, the tenancy drafts, the letters, that's most of my week, and AI does it faster. I'd probably keep my job because farmers trust a face, but the work would shrink and so would the chance of a pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools once a couple of colleagues had them working, probably within six months. I'd spend more time out on farms, meeting families, because that's what the software can't do. And I'd start putting fifty a month aside, even if it means no holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit anxious. Like a wet harvest: you can't stop it, you just manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our secretary, Gwen, who's done the property paperwork for thirty years. And the other junior lawyer, who's lovely but hates going out to farms. If I'm honest, I'd rather it was him than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. What if the work shrank and you lost your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go home and work on the farm with my brother for a while. That's what families are for. I'd rather muck out cows on my brother's farm than claim benefits.

say: I'd say handle it **sensibly**, without panic or handouts.
I'd say farmers have coped with **new machines** for a hundred years.
think: Registry checks and **tenancy drafts** are most of my week, and AI does them faster.
I'd likely keep my job, but the **work and pay rise** would shrink.
do: Learn the **AI tools** within six months, once colleagues have them working.
Spend more time on **farm visits** meeting families.
Put **fifty a month** aside, even without a holiday.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **anxious**, like a wet harvest you just manage.
S1.quote: I'd rather muck out cows on my brother's farm than claim benefits.
fieldNote: She expects **hours and pay** to shrink, not an outright job loss.
She admits she'd rather a **colleague** went than her.
Her safety net is **family**, not the state.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools once colleagues have them working
Spend more time on farm visits meeting families
Put fifty a month aside and skip the holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together. The government should slow firms down from sacking everyone at once, but people will have to look after their own. I'd say it at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years and my job is gone, or near enough. Farm law is reading deeds and writing agreements, all thinking work, so 2028 is my date. My brother's farm gets three years more because it's hands-on, but even he does his planning and orders on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my brother in the first month about coming back to the farm part time, doing the books, the paperwork and the milking rota. My boyfriend and I would give up the cottage and move into the old farm worker's house rent-free. I'd keep my law job as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sad, too. I worked so hard to be the one who got out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say the farm was always there for me. My mum would worry I'd wasted law school. Both would be right, which is the hard bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your boyfriend's job at the tractor dealer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He fixes machines, so he'd last a few more years, maybe till the robots fix the robots. Then it's both of us on the farm. A dairy farm can feed a family, but it can't pay two wages.

say: I'd say families and **communities** will have to pull together.
I'd want firms slowed from **sacking everyone** at once.
think: Farm law is all thinking work, so **2028 is my date**.
My brother's farm gets **three more years**, though his planning moves to screens.
do: Ask my brother about **part-time farm work** in the first month.
**Move** into the old farm worker's house rent-free.
Keep my **law job** as long as they'll have me.
feel: **Alarmed** and **sad**, after working so hard to get out.
S2.quote: A dairy farm can feed a family, but it can't pay two wages.
fieldNote: She clearly sees the **thinking-first, robots-later** order in her own family.
Going back to the farm feels like **undoing** her escape.
Her boyfriend's mechanic job buys **a few years**, no more.

steps.text: Ask her brother about part-time farm work on books and rotas
Move into the old farm worker's house rent-free
Keep her law job as long as the firm keeps her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are sensible. Learn the tools, save, keep family close. Farms and small towns will look after themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a chance to become the lawyer farmers trust to check what the computer says. I'd be 32, maybe married by then. I'm not the cleverest, but I know the families, and that might count for a few extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly in the first year, once the firm settles on one. I'd save a hundred a month and aim for three months by 2030. And I'd talk to my boyfriend about getting married and moving closer to the farm, so we have a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control. It's like seeing rain coming and getting the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why get married sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were going to anyway. With five years to plan, I'd rather we did it properly, in the church, before things get hard. It's one less thing to sort when the work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said knowing the families might count for a few extra years. Would it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the older generation, yes. The old farmers want a lawyer they've known since school, but their children are the ones selling land in 2031. Their children will use whatever's cheapest.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to prepare** if people are sensible.
I'd say **learn the tools**, save and keep family close.
think: I could become the lawyer farmers trust to **check the computer**.
Knowing **the families** might buy a few extra years.
do: Learn the firm's **AI tools** properly in year one.
Save **a hundred a month**, aiming for three months by 2030.
Marry and **move closer** to the farm as a fallback.
feel: **Anxious but in control**, like getting the hay in before rain.
S3.quote: The old farmers want a lawyer they've known since school, but their children are the ones selling land in 2031.
fieldNote: She sees her edge, **local trust**, fading with the next generation.
Five years lets her **plan family steps** around the change.
She would adopt tools once **proven**, true to her steady nature.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools properly in the first year
Save a hundred a month to reach three months by 2030
Marry in the church and move closer to the family farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good warning, and nobody has an excuse not to prepare. Young people should learn a trade or a skill that's hard to automate. The government shouldn't need to do much if people plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels all right for me. I'd be 37, with a farm in the family and a decade of knowing every family in the valley. I'd still worry about money, because a decade of low pay doesn't build much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm and pick up the AI tools as they become normal. I'd do a short course in farm business management by 2028, so I could advise families or run the farm side if needed. And I'd keep fifty a month going into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now and then, mostly fine. The farm is my safety net, and I'm grateful for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother want you on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes, and then we'd argue about the cows. We get on, but we're both stubborn. I'd want to be useful there, not a guest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years of low pay. What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much left to give up, honestly. We don't go abroad, we don't eat out. Maybe the second car, if my boyfriend could get a lift to the dealer.

say: I'd say ten years is **good warning** with no excuse not to prepare.
I'd tell young people to learn a skill **hard to automate**.
think: Ten years feels **all right**, with the farm and the valley behind me.
**Low pay** for a decade still doesn't build much.
do: Pick up the **AI tools** as they become normal.
Keep **fifty a month** going into savings.
feel: **Uneasy** now and then, grateful for the **farm** as a net.
S4.quote: The farm is my safety net, and I'm grateful for it.
fieldNote: A decade plus the **family farm** keeps her own job feeling safe for now.
She'd want to be **useful** on the farm, not a guest.
There's **little left to cut**, which limits her saving.

steps.text: Pick up the AI tools as they become normal at the firm
Take a short farm business management course by 2028
Keep fifty a month going into savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, and my job and my boyfriend's go one after the other, with the farm trying to hold us all. What would help is time, honestly, and firms having to give proper notice, plus farm business courses that don't cost the earth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the countryside. People talk about AI in cities, but out here, one firm closing means there's no lawyer for thirty miles.

headlineQuote: Out here, one firm closing means there's no lawyer for thirty miles.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** farm and land lawyer at a small rural firm, from a **dairy family**.
She rents a cottage with her boyfriend, a tractor mechanic, and has **under a month** saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once colleagues show they're safe.
She rejects handouts and treats her brother's **farm** as the family safety net.
Her mood peaks at **alarmed** for AGI by 2028, when her job and her boyfriend's go in turn.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her job and her boyfriend's going one after the other.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, and firms having to give proper notice.
